summary: Defines signature policies for electronic signatures. A policy is a set of rules for creating and validating a signature, and a legal or contractual context may accept one as meeting its needs. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3125 defines a signature policy, which is a written set of rules for making and checking an electronic signature. The signer names the policy inside the signature, so the person checking it later knows exactly which rules apply and reaches the same result.

questions: what is an electronic signature policy
what is a signature policy identifier
how does a verifier use a signature policy
what is a signature validation policy
subtitle: A written rulebook for creating and checking electronic signatures, so both sides reach the same verdict.

tldr.problem: Two parties checking an electronic signature can reach different conclusions, because nothing fixes the rules they apply or says which rules the signer meant to follow.
tldr.mechanism: A signature policy is a set of rules for creating and validating a signature, identified by a globally unique Object Identifier that the signer binds into the signature along with a hash of the policy text.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental document whose content is based on the signature policy in ETSI TS 101 733. It defines an ASN.1 structure for a machine readable policy, and leaves the choice of form to the issuer.

today: RFC 3125 is an Experimental document from September 2001, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo states that its content is based on the signature policy defined in ETSI TS 101 733 V.1.2.2, and it leaves the choice of the policy's form to the issuer while offering an ASN.1 structure for a machine readable one.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 3125 covers signature policies usable with electronic signatures in many kinds of transaction, such as purchase requisitions, contracts and invoices, and for transactions between an individual and a company, between two companies, or between an individual and a governmental body. The document is independent of any environment. It can be applied to smart cards, GSM SIM cards, or special programs for electronic signatures.

The memo defines a signature policy as a set of rules for the creation and validation of an electronic signature, under which the validity of the signature can be determined. A given legal or contractual context may recognize a particular signature policy as meeting its requirements. The policy must be available in human readable form so that it can be assessed against the legal and contractual context in which it is applied, and it needs another part that states the electronic rules for creating and validating the signature in a form a computer can process. The memo defines that format using ASN.1, and says that future versions may include a structured specification using XML. The content is based on the signature policy defined in ETSI TS 101 733 V.1.2.2.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo gives organizations a way to publish the rules they will use for electronic signatures. The rules have to be readable by people, because a court or a contract may check them, and readable by a computer, because the checking is automated.

sections.title: The Parties
sections.content:
The memo names five parties. The Signature Policy Issuer, which is a Trusted Service Provider, issues the signature policies that define the technical and procedural requirements for creating and validating electronic signatures so that a particular business need is met. The Signer is the entity that creates the electronic signature; when the signer digitally signs over a signature policy identifier, it makes a commitment on behalf of the signing entity that the data being signed is signed under the rules defined by that policy. The Verifier is the entity that validates the electronic signature, and it may be a single entity or several. The verifier MUST validate the signature under the rules defined by the signature policy for the signature to be valid. The Arbitrator settles disputes between a signer and a verifier, acting as verifier when it checks a signature that has already been validated.

The Trusted Service Providers are one or more entities that help build trust relationships between the signer and the verifier, and a policy may mandate the use of their services. Those services include user certificates, cross-certificates, time-stamping tokens, CRLs, ARLs and OCSP responses. The memo also names the supporting parties: Certification Authorities, which give users public key certificates; Registration Authorities, which register entities before a CA issues certificates; Repository Authorities, which publish CRLs, cross-certificates, signature policies and optionally leaf certificates; Time-Stamping Authorities, which attest that some data existed before a given trusted time; One-line Certificate Status Protocol responders, which report whether a particular certificate is revoked, not revoked or unknown; and Attribute Authorities, which give users attributes linked to public key certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: Five roles matter here. One organisation writes the rules. One party signs under them. One party checks the signature later. A fourth settles disputes, and a fifth supplies certificates, revocation lists and time-stamps that the check needs.

sections.title: The Structure of a Signature Policy
sections.content:
The memo mandates that an electronic signature must be processed by the signer and the verifier in accordance with the signature policy referenced by the signer; that the policy must be identifiable by an Object Identifier; that a specification of the policy must exist; that for a given policy there must be one definitive form of the specification with a unique binary encoding; and that a hash of that definitive specification, using an agreed algorithm, must be provided by the signer and checked by the verifier. The memo does not mandate the form of the specification itself: it may be a free form document for human interpretation or a structured form using an agreed syntax and encoding.

The optional ASN.1 structure is encoded using the Distinguished Encoding Rules. The policy information is preceded by an identifier for the hashing algorithm used to protect the policy and followed by the hash value, which must be recalculated and checked whenever the policy passes between the issuer and the signer or verifier. The hash is calculated without the outer type and length fields. Inside, SignPolicyInfo holds the policy identifier as an Object Identifier, the date of issue, the name of the policy issuer in one or more general name forms, a description of the expected application of the policy, the signature validation policy, and an optional set of extensions that is a generic way to extend any sub-component of a signature policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Each policy carries a unique name, the date it was issued, who issued it, what it is for, and the rules themselves. The signer also attaches a fingerprint of the policy text, so the checker can confirm it is reading the same rules the signer did.

sections.title: The Validation Rules
sections.content:
The signature validation policy says which data elements the signer must put in a signature and which the verifier must find for the signature to be potentially valid. It begins with the signing period, which identifies the date and time before which the policy should not be used and an optional date after which it should not be used. Then come the common rules, which apply to all commitment types, and the commitment rules, which apply to given commitment types.

The common rules hold the trust conditions for certificates, time-stamps and attributes, together with any constraints on attributes that may be included in the electronic signature. If a field is present in the common rules then the equivalent field must not be present in any of the commitment rules, and if the signer and verifier rules, the signing certificate trust condition or the time-stamp trust condition are missing from the common rules then they must be present in each commitment rule. A commitment rule lists the commitment types it covers. If the selected commitment types indicate empty, the rule applies when a commitment type is not present, which is the case where the type of commitment is indicated in the semantics of the message. Otherwise the signature must carry a commitment type indication that fits one of the listed types, and a specific commitment type identifier must not appear in more than one rule.

Trust conditions are given for three things. The signing certificate trust condition holds the trust points used to start and end certificate path processing plus the revocation requirements. The time-stamp trust condition adds naming constraints on the time-stamping authority, a caution period after which the verifier must wait before it can be confident that the signer's key was secure and that any revocation has been notified, and a maximum acceptable delay between the signing time and the time the signature time-stamp is created. The attribute trust condition says whether certified attributes are required, and whether the signer's own claimed attributes are acceptable or only attributes carried in attribute certificates.

The algorithm constraints name the signing algorithms that may be used for each purpose, with any minimum key length, and apply to the signer, to issuers of end entity certificates, to issuers of CA certificates, to attribute authorities and to time-stamping authorities. If the field is absent the policy applies no constraints. Additional rules may be added to any of the structures, using an ASN.1 extension with an associated object identifier and a DER encoded value.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules cover a period during which signatures may be made, the kinds of commitment a signature may carry, which certificates and time-stamps count as trustworthy, and which algorithms and key lengths are allowed. A verifier reads these rules and applies them to the signature in front of it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo has two points to make. The first is that the security of the electronic signature mechanism depends on the privacy of the signer's private key, and that implementations must take steps to ensure that private keys cannot be compromised.

The second is about algorithms. Implementers should be aware that cryptographic algorithms become weaker with time, because new cryptanalysis techniques are developed and computing performance improves, so the work factor needed to break a particular algorithm falls. Implementations should therefore be modular, allowing new algorithms to be inserted readily, and implementers should be prepared for the set of mandatory to implement algorithms to change over time.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything rests on the signer's private key staying secret. And because old cryptography weakens over time, the rules name algorithms in a way that lets them be replaced later without rewriting the whole policy.

sections.title: Conformance Requirements
sections.content:
The conformance requirement is one sentence: signer and verifier systems shall be able to process an electronic signature in accordance with the specification of the signature policy identified by an Object Identifier.

The annexes describe two ways to implement that. One is a validation process that supports one specific policy, given by its Object Identifier, conforming to a human readable description whose processing rules are clearly defined. That may be simpler to build at first, but it becomes harder to extend to many policies, because each additional policy needs its own customisation. The other is a validation process that is dynamically programmable and adapts its validation rules from a description of the policy in a computer-processable language, which is what the ASN.1 structure provides. That kind of implementation can support many policies without being modified each time, provided all the rules the policy specifies are known to it.
sections.plainLanguage: A signer and a checker must both work from the same published policy. The annexes offer two ways to build the checker: one that knows a single policy, and one that reads any policy written in the machine readable form.

viz.caption: THE FIVE PARTIES NAMED IN THE MEMO

items.title: Signature Policy Issuer
items.text: Publishes the policy that defines how signatures are made and checked.

items.title: Signer
items.text: Creates the signature and names the policy it was made under.

items.title: Verifier
items.text: Checks the signature against the rules in that policy.

items.title: Arbitrator
items.text: Settles disputes between a signer and a verifier.

items.title: Trusted Service Provider
items.text: Supplies certificates, revocation lists and time-stamps the check needs.

viz.caption: THE ASN.1 STRUCTURE OF A SIGNATURE POLICY
THE REVOCATION CHECKS A POLICY CAN REQUIRE

items.label: clrCheck
items.desc: Checks must be made against current CRLs or authority revocation lists.

items.label: ocspCheck
items.desc: The revocation status must be checked using the Online Certificate Status Protocol.

items.label: bothCheck
items.desc: Both CRL and OCSP checks must be carried out.

items.label: eitherCheck
items.desc: At least one of the CRL or OCSP checks must be carried out.

items.label: other
items.desc: Another mechanism, as defined by a signature policy extension.
